title: Lifting the scroll
hookLine: the open scroll is raised high for everyone to see

cards: A person walks up to the reading table and takes hold of the two wooden rollers of an open Torah scroll. It's heavy, and open several columns wide.

They slide it to the edge, bend their knees, and in one motion lift it high overhead, arms spread, the letters facing the room. Then they turn slowly, so everyone can see. Some people stretch out a finger toward it.
Some sing. Nobody breathes much until it's safely down.

teach.b: It's called hagbah, lifting. The lifter raises the scroll open, often wide enough that at least three columns show, and turns so every part of the room can see the writing.
A later rabbinic handbook for scribes, tractate Soferim, describes the scroll shown to everyone, men and women, so all could see the letters and bow.

teach.h: THIS IS THE TORAH MOSES SET BEFORE US.
teach.b: As it rises, the congregation sings: this is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel. The first half comes from Deuteronomy.
In the old Jewish translation: "And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel." It echoes a much older scene.

When Ezra the scribe gathered the people in Jerusalem, the book of Nehemiah says he opened the book in the sight of all the people, "and when he opened it, all the people stood up." The timing differs.
In most Ashkenazi communities, the lifting comes after the reading; in most Sephardi communities, before. Then a second person, the golel, rolls the scroll closed and dresses it again in its cover.
The Talmud, in Megillah 32a, gives that rolling a surprising honor: the one who rolls the scroll receives the reward of all the readers. So the text isn't just read to people.
It's shown: lifted out of the experts' hands and turned toward everyone, so the whole room can see it's real.

how: At hagbah, one person lifts the open Torah scroll and turns to show the congregation, who sing V'zot haTorah; in most Ashkenazi communities this follows the reading and in most Sephardi communities it precedes it, and a second person, the golel, rolls and dresses the scroll.

games.q: you've just lifted the open Torah high above your head. the room is singing. what do you do next?
o: turn slowly so every side of the room can see the writing.
read a verse aloud from it.
games.why: hagbah is about showing: the lifter turns so everyone can see the letters, then sits to let the golel roll it closed.

practice: Think of something you love that other people rarely get to see: a book that changed you, a grandmother's recipe, a song, a skill you're quietly good at.
Picture holding it up for one person, not explaining it to death, just turning it toward them so they can see it for themselves.

wordCard.voice: Hagbah. Lifting. The open Torah scroll raised high and turned so everyone in the room can see the writing.

orig.note: Hebrew: lifting. often shortened in speech to hagbah.

carryVoice: Your line: lift it up. What's held high is meant for the whole room. Day five hundred ninety-nine, done.
